name: Blount Disease

criteria.description: Progressive varus deformity of the proximal tibia
Irregularity and fragmentation of the medial proximal tibial epiphysis on imaging
Onset typically before 10 years of age, often in toddlers
Exclusion of metabolic bone diseases such as rickets

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of progressive proximal tibial varus deformity with characteristic medial tibial epiphyseal irregularities on imaging in a child under 10 years old, excluding metabolic bone diseases
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Radiographic staging (Langenskiöld classification) is often used to assess severity.

common.symptomName: Abnormality of the proximal tibial epiphysis

laboratory: Normal serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D levels (to exclude rickets)
imaging: Radiographs showing medial proximal tibial epiphyseal irregularity and fragmentation
Langenskiöld classification stages I-VI on X-ray
MRI may show physeal and metaphyseal changes
genetic: No specific genetic mutation identified; multifactorial etiology with possible genetic predisposition
other: Clinical observation of progressive varus deformity

distinguishingFeatures: Absence of epiphyseal fragmentation on imaging
Abnormal laboratory values (low vitamin D, calcium, phosphate)
Widened growth plates with cupping and fraying on X-ray
Systemic signs of metabolic bone disease
Genetic testing positive for specific mutations

redFlags: Rapidly progressive varus deformity beyond toddler age
Failure to respond to conservative management
references: Sabharwal S. Blount disease. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2009;91(5):1758-1776.
Langenskiöld A. Tibia vara. A survey of seventy-one cases treated with osteotomy. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1964;46:1405-1420.
